lessons.title: Context: 18th-Century England & the Foundling Hospital
lessons.description: Thomas Coram, the Foundling Hospital, child trafficking and Georgian class system.
lessons.content_html:
Why Context Matters for Coram Boy

Jamila Gavin’s Coram Boy (2000) is set in Georgian England, a period of stark contrasts between wealth and poverty, refinement and cruelty. The novel spans approximately 1741–1750 and draws heavily on real historical events and places. For the Edexcel exam, you must weave contextual knowledge throughout your essay — not bolt it on as a separate paragraph — to show you understand how the setting shapes characters and themes.

Key Fact

Edexcel assesses AO3 (context) heavily in Section B. You must connect historical facts about 18th-century England directly to how Gavin presents characters, settings and themes in the novel.

Thomas Coram and the Foundling Hospital

Captain Thomas Coram was a retired sea captain who was horrified by the sight of abandoned babies and children on London’s streets. After seventeen years of campaigning, he persuaded wealthy patrons to fund the Foundling Hospital, which opened in 1739 in Bloomsbury, London. It was the world’s first incorporated charity and the UK’s oldest children’s charity. Mothers who could not care for their babies could leave them at the Hospital, where they would be given a new name, educated and trained for employment.

In the novel, the Foundling Hospital becomes a place of salvation for Aaron (Toby), contrasting sharply with the fate of babies who fall into Otis Gardiner’s hands. Gavin uses this real institution to explore the theme of how society chooses which children deserve protection and which are disposable.

The composer George Frideric Handel was one of the Foundling Hospital’s most important benefactors. He conducted annual performances of his Messiah at the Hospital from 1750, raising thousands of pounds. In Coram Boy, Handel is a living character whose music runs through the narrative like a thread. Gavin uses Handel and his music to represent beauty, redemption and the possibility of transcending one’s birth — Aaron’s musical talent connects him to this world of art and grace, despite his origins as an abandoned child.

Abandoned Children and Child Trafficking

In 18th-century England, thousands of unwanted children were abandoned each year. Illegitimate children faced social disgrace and were often left to die. Before the Foundling Hospital, there was virtually no institutional support for these children. Some were taken in by baby farmers who charged a fee but frequently neglected or killed the children entrusted to them.

Gavin draws on this dark reality through the character of Otis Gardiner, who collects babies from desperate mothers for a fee, promising to deliver them to the Foundling Hospital. In reality, Otis and his son Meshak bury most of these babies in the countryside. This child trafficking plot is not invention — it reflects documented 18th-century practices where unscrupulous individuals exploited vulnerable mothers for profit.

Key Fact

Baby farming was a real and widespread practice in 18th-century England. Gavin uses Otis Gardiner’s child-collecting scheme to dramatise how the most vulnerable members of society — infants and unmarried mothers — were exploited for profit.

Class, Wealth and the Social Hierarchy

Georgian England had a rigid class system. The landed gentry like the Ashbrooks lived in grand country estates, while the urban poor lived in squalor. The gap between rich and poor is central to Coram Boy: Alexander Ashbrook grows up in privilege at Ashbrook House in Gloucestershire, while Meshak and the foundling children exist at the very bottom of society. Gavin uses these contrasts to explore whether a person’s worth is determined by birth or by character.

The novel is set during the height of the transatlantic slave trade. Gavin includes Toby, a Black child at the Foundling Hospital, to remind the reader that the exploitation of children was part of a wider culture of treating human beings as property. The character of Mrs Lynch also references the slave trade through her connections. By weaving slavery into the narrative, Gavin broadens her exploration of who in 18th-century society was considered fully human and who was not.

Gavin’s Purpose: Why This Context Matters

Gavin wrote Coram Boy in 2000, drawing on years of historical research. She was born in India and grew up in England, and her work frequently explores the experiences of outsiders and marginalised groups. By choosing to set her novel in 18th-century England, Gavin invites the modern reader to see parallels between historical and contemporary attitudes to children, poverty and race. The novel was adapted for the stage by the National Theatre in 2005, receiving four Olivier Award nominations including Best New Play, which brought Gavin’s themes to an even wider audience.

Understanding this historical context is not optional for the exam — it is how you unlock the deeper meanings of Gavin’s novel. Every character, every setting and every plot event connects back to the realities of 18th-century England. When you write about the Foundling Hospital, the class system, child trafficking or slavery, you are engaging with AO3 — and demonstrating that you understand the world Gavin recreates and why she chose to recreate it.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In the Edexcel English Literature exam, Section B questions on Coram Boy will always be preceded by a short quotation. You do not need to have memorised the exact quote beforehand, but you must respond to it and use it as a springboard for your essay. AO3 (context) is worth significant marks, so embed historical knowledge — about the Foundling Hospital, class system, child trafficking and slavery — directly into your analysis of characters and themes, rather than writing a separate ‘context paragraph’.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Coram Boy is set in Georgian England (1741–1750), a period of extreme inequality, where abandoned children, baby farming and the slave trade were everyday realities.
  • The Foundling Hospital, founded by Thomas Coram in 1739, is central to the novel — it represents both salvation and the question of which children society chooses to save.
  • Handel’s music connects the novel’s themes of beauty, redemption and transcendence, and his real historical involvement with the Foundling Hospital grounds the fiction in fact.

lessons.title: Part 1: Meshak, Otis & the Coram Men
lessons.description: Otis Gardiner's scheme, Meshak's innocence, the buried babies and the Ashbrooks.
lessons.content_html:
Part 1: The Coram Men

The first part of Coram Boy introduces two worlds that could not be more different: the dark, wandering life of Otis Gardiner and his son Meshak, and the privileged Ashbrook household in Gloucestershire. Gavin uses parallel narratives to build dramatic tension and explore how children’s fates are determined by the adults around them.

Otis Gardiner: The Villain

Otis Gardiner travels the English countryside posing as a ‘Coram man’ — someone who collects babies on behalf of the Foundling Hospital. Desperate mothers, often unmarried women facing social ruin, pay Otis to take their babies to safety. But Otis has no connection to the Foundling Hospital. He pockets the money and orders his son Meshak to bury the babies in fields and ditches along the road.

Key Fact

Otis Gardiner exploits both the mothers and the babies. He represents a society where the most vulnerable are treated as commodities — their lives have a price but no value. Gavin presents Otis as a product of a system that abandons its weakest members.

Gavin does not present Otis as a cartoonish villain. He is calculating, manipulative and utterly without remorse. His cruelty is made more disturbing by its ordinariness — he treats child trafficking as a business, no different from selling goods at market. This banality of evil is one of the novel’s most powerful features. Otis controls every aspect of Meshak’s life through fear and intimidation, exploiting his son’s disability and dependence. The father-son relationship between Otis and Meshak is a dark inversion of the parent-child bonds that the novel elsewhere celebrates.

Meshak: Innocence Trapped

Meshak is Otis’s son, a young man with a learning disability who is entirely dependent on his father. He is terrified of Otis and haunted by the babies he has been forced to bury. Gavin presents Meshak with great sympathy — he is gentle, loving and deeply moral, but trapped in a situation he cannot escape. His innocence makes Otis’s crimes even more horrifying, because the reader sees them through Meshak’s bewildered, grief-stricken eyes.

When Meshak discovers the baby born to Melissa and Alexander, he sees the child as an angel — beautiful and precious. Instead of burying this baby as Otis commands, Meshak secretly saves the child, taking him to the Foundling Hospital. This act of defiance is the turning point of the novel. Meshak’s decision to save Aaron shows that goodness can exist even within a system of terrible evil. Gavin uses Meshak to argue that moral courage is not linked to intelligence or status — Meshak, the character society would dismiss as worthless, is the one who saves a life.

Alexander Ashbrook and Melissa

Alexander Ashbrook is the son of Sir William Ashbrook, a wealthy Gloucestershire landowner. Alexander is passionate about music and dreams of studying under Handel in London, but his father insists he follow a respectable career. This conflict between duty and passion drives Alexander’s storyline. Alexander falls in love with Melissa, and their secret relationship produces a baby. When Melissa’s family discover the pregnancy, the baby is given to Otis — unwittingly condemning the child to what should be death.

Key Fact

Alexander and Melissa’s baby is the child Meshak saves — the baby who becomes Aaron at the Foundling Hospital. This connection between the Ashbrook family and the foundling world is hidden from the characters but visible to the reader, creating powerful dramatic irony.

The scenes where Meshak buries babies are written in a Gothic style — dark landscapes, nighttime, isolation and horror. Gavin uses Gothic imagery to force the reader to confront what is happening rather than look away. The earth itself seems to reject the crime: Meshak hears the babies crying in his mind long after they are buried. These hauntings blur the line between psychological trauma and the supernatural, adding a layer of unease that runs through the entire novel.

The Role of Part 1 in the Novel’s Structure

Part 1 establishes the novel’s central tension: the collision between a world of privilege and a world of exploitation, connected by the fate of one child. Gavin shows that these two worlds are not separate — they depend on each other, because the comfort of the wealthy is built on the suffering of the poor.

Structurally, Part 1 plants the seeds of every major conflict that will unfold later. Alexander’s passion for music will reappear through Aaron’s singing voice. Meshak’s secret act of defiance will have consequences that echo across decades. Otis’s crimes will eventually be exposed. Every key event in Parts 2 and 3 has its origin here, making Part 1 essential to understanding the novel as a whole. In the exam, being able to trace these connections across the text demonstrates the kind of structural awareness that earns high AO1 marks.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When writing about Part 1 of Coram Boy, always link plot events to their thematic significance. Don’t just narrate what happens — explain why Gavin presents it this way. For example, rather than saying ‘Meshak buries the babies’, write: ‘Gavin uses the Gothic imagery of Meshak burying the babies to confront the reader with the dehumanising reality of child trafficking, forcing us to see what 18th-century society chose to ignore.’ This analytical approach is what earns AO1 marks.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Otis Gardiner poses as a ‘Coram man’ to exploit desperate mothers, pocketing their money and disposing of their babies — representing the banality of evil in a society that commodifies children.
  • Meshak’s decision to save Alexander and Melissa’s baby is the novel’s pivotal act of moral courage, showing that goodness is not linked to intelligence or social status.
  • Gavin uses parallel narratives and dramatic irony to connect the privileged Ashbrook world to the dark underworld of child trafficking, revealing that these worlds are interdependent.

lessons.title: Part 2: The Foundling Hospital
lessons.description: Aaron and Toby at the Foundling Hospital, Handel's music, class divisions and the Coram boys' lives.
lessons.content_html:
Part 2: Life at the Foundling Hospital

The second part of Coram Boy jumps forward in time. The baby Meshak saved is now a boy called Toby — later known as Aaron — growing up at the Foundling Hospital in London. He has no knowledge of his true parents or how he came to be there. Alongside him is his closest friend, also called Toby, a Black child. Gavin uses the Foundling Hospital setting to explore themes of identity, belonging and how institutions shape children’s lives.

Key Fact

At the real Foundling Hospital, children were given new names and identities. Their birth names were never used, and mothers were not told what their child was renamed. Gavin uses this historical detail to develop the theme of lost identity — Aaron does not know who he truly is.

The Foundling Hospital Regime

Life at the Foundling Hospital was structured and disciplined. Children were clothed in a uniform, educated to a basic level and trained in skills that would prepare them for apprenticeship. Boys were typically apprenticed to tradesmen or sent into the navy; girls went into domestic service. The Hospital was a charity, not a family — the children were cared for, but they were not loved in the way a parent loves a child.

Gavin shows both the kindness and the limitations of institutional care. Aaron is safe, fed and educated, but he has no parents, no surname and no knowledge of where he comes from. The Hospital saves his life but cannot give him an identity. This tension between institutional rescue and emotional absence runs through Part 2.

When mothers left their babies at the real Foundling Hospital, they often left a token — a coin, a scrap of fabric, a button or a piece of ribbon. These tokens were recorded in the Hospital’s registers and kept in case a mother ever returned to claim her child. In the novel, the concept of the token symbolises the fragile thread connecting Aaron to his origins. He possesses no token, no clue about who his parents are — this absence drives his search for identity in Part 2 and beyond.

Handel’s Music and Aaron’s Gift

Music is the thread that connects Aaron to his father Alexander, though neither of them knows it. Aaron has an extraordinary musical gift, particularly as a singer. When Handel visits the Foundling Hospital to conduct rehearsals for his annual Messiah performance, he discovers Aaron’s voice and recognises his exceptional talent. This mirrors how, years earlier, Alexander Ashbrook defied his father to pursue music under Handel’s guidance.

Gavin uses music as a motif throughout the novel. For Aaron, music represents the possibility that talent and beauty can transcend the circumstances of birth. His voice is proof that he is more than his status as a foundling — it is the invisible inheritance from his father. For the exam, analysing the motif of music allows you to connect character, theme and structure in a single argument.

Key Fact

Aaron’s musical gift is inherited from Alexander — it is the invisible thread connecting father and son across the novel’s two parts. Gavin uses music to argue that identity is not just about names and paperwork, but about deeper, inherited qualities.

Class and the Foundling Boys

The foundling boys occupy an ambiguous position in the class system. They are not poor street children — the Hospital gives them education and respectability — but they are not gentlemen either. They have no family name, no inheritance and no social connections. In 18th-century England, where your family name determined everything, the foundlings exist in a kind of social limbo.

Aaron’s friend Toby is a Black child at the Foundling Hospital. Gavin includes Toby to highlight that the foundling children came from all backgrounds and that the exploitation of children intersected with the exploitation of enslaved people. Toby’s presence raises questions about race and belonging in 18th-century London, where Black people were present but marginalised. Through Toby, Gavin adds another layer to the novel’s exploration of who society considers worthy of care and protection.

Education and Apprenticeship

The Foundling Hospital gave children a basic education in reading, writing and arithmetic. Boys were typically apprenticed to tradesmen such as weavers, shoemakers or rope-makers at around fourteen. Girls were sent into domestic service. The intention was to produce useful, self-supporting members of society — not scholars or gentlemen. Gavin uses this detail to highlight the ceiling placed on foundling children: they could survive, but they could not rise. Aaron’s musical talent threatens to break this pattern, which is why Handel’s recognition of his voice is so significant — it offers a path that the institution was never designed to provide.

Part 2 deepens the novel’s central questions: can a person find identity without knowing their origins? Can talent and character overcome the limitations of class? And what happens when the truth about someone’s past begins to surface?

This kind of structural analysis across the whole text is what earns the highest AO1 marks. Always connect to AO3 by explaining what the Foundling Hospital was really like and why foundling children occupied such an unusual social position.

Key Takeaways

  • Part 2 centres on Aaron (Toby) growing up at the Foundling Hospital with no knowledge of his parents, exploring the tension between institutional care and emotional belonging.
  • Music is the motif that connects Aaron to his father Alexander — his inherited talent proves that identity runs deeper than names or social status.
  • The foundling boys exist in social limbo — neither destitute nor gentlemen — and Gavin uses their position to question how class determines a person’s worth in 18th-century England.

lessons.title: Part 3: Discovery & Resolution
lessons.content_html:
Part 3: Discovery and Resolution

The final part of Coram Boy brings the novel’s two worlds crashing together. Secrets that have been hidden for years are uncovered, and characters must confront the truth about who Aaron really is. Gavin builds towards a climax that is both thrilling and emotionally devastating, weaving together the threads of parentage, revelation, sacrifice and justice.

Aaron’s Parentage Revealed

The central revelation of Part 3 is that Aaron — the foundling boy with the extraordinary singing voice — is the son of Alexander Ashbrook and Melissa. For years, Alexander has believed his child died. Melissa has carried the grief of losing her baby in silence. The discovery that their son is alive, and has been living at the Foundling Hospital under a different name, is the novel’s emotional core.

Key Fact

The revelation of Aaron’s parentage resolves the dramatic irony that has run throughout the novel. The reader has known since Part 1 that Meshak saved the baby, but Alexander, Melissa and Aaron himself have been kept in the dark. When the truth finally emerges, it is both a release of tension and a moment of profound emotional impact.

Gavin handles the reunion with restraint. It is not a simple happy ending — years have been lost, identities have been fractured, and the damage done by Otis’s crimes cannot be fully undone. Alexander must reconcile the privileged world he inhabits with the foundling world his son has grown up in. Aaron must absorb the fact that his entire identity — his name, his history, his place in society — has been a fiction.

Thomas Ledbury’s Sacrifice

The novel’s climax turns on a moment of devastating sacrifice — but the hero who dies is not Meshak. It is Thomas Ledbury, Alexander’s loyal childhood friend, who is shot and killed by Gaddarn (Otis) during the rescue of Aaron and Toby. Thomas comes to the waterfront to help free the boys, and Gavin uses his death to show that ordinary decency, not great wealth or social standing, is what defines true courage. Meshak, by contrast, survives the climax: having defied his father years earlier by saving the baby, he lives to see Aaron safe. In the Epilogue, Meshak dies peacefully of old age, his final thoughts resting on the child he once rescued. It is Thomas’s death, not Meshak’s, that constitutes the novel’s act of physical sacrifice.

Thomas Ledbury’s death is one of the novel’s most powerful moments. He is not a grand or glamorous character — he is a reliable, loyal friend who acts when it matters most. Gavin uses his death to argue that moral courage is found in ordinary people, not in the wealthy or powerful who failed Aaron throughout his life. Yet Meshak’s arc carries its own profound weight. The character whom society would consider the least valuable — a man with a learning disability, the son of a criminal — shows the deepest selflessness: he saved Aaron as a baby at great personal risk, watched over him for years, and in the Epilogue dies peacefully knowing the boy is safe. Together, Thomas and Meshak represent Gavin’s argument that human worth cannot be measured by class, intelligence, or social standing.

Otis’s Villainy Exposed

The truth about Otis Gardiner’s child-collecting scheme is finally brought to light. His years of deception — posing as a Coram man, taking money from desperate mothers, ordering the burial of babies — are exposed. But Gavin deliberately refuses to give Otis a clean villain’s justice. He had already escaped hanging earlier in the novel by bribing officials to hang another man in his place, then reinvented himself as the wealthy Philip Gaddarn. In the climactic boat scene, Gaddarn falls or disappears overboard during the chaos of the rescue — his ultimate fate is left deliberately ambiguous. This is not accident or oversight: Gavin’s point is that the system which enabled Otis’s crimes remains intact even after he is gone.

Key Fact

Gavin deliberately withholds clean justice for Otis. He escapes the noose by having an innocent man hanged in his place, operates for years as Philip Gaddarn, and then vanishes into the water during the climax. His ultimate fate is unknown. Gavin’s point is not that villainy always meets punishment, but that the social and economic systems that made Otis’s crimes possible continue long after he is gone. The true drama of the resolution belongs to Thomas Ledbury’s sacrifice and Aaron’s reunion with his parents.

Resolution and Justice

The novel’s ending offers a qualified sense of resolution. Aaron is reunited with his birth parents. Otis’s crimes are exposed and Thomas Ledbury gives his life in the rescue. The buried babies are finally acknowledged. But Gavin does not present this as an uncomplicated happy ending. Thomas is dead. Aaron must absorb the shattering truth about his origins. The years he spent without a family cannot be returned. The other babies Otis buried are gone forever. And Otis himself — now Gaddarn — disappears overboard, his fate unknown, the system that created him unchanged. Justice comes, but it is partial, costly, and incomplete.

The ending asks the reader to hold two truths at once: that justice is possible, and that it is never complete. Aaron gains a family but has lost his foundling identity. Thomas Ledbury’s courage saves Aaron and Toby but costs him his life. Meshak survives to die peacefully in old age, his final peace a quiet form of redemption. Otis’s crimes are exposed, but he slips away rather than facing justice, and the system that enabled him — the class inequality, the lack of protection for vulnerable mothers and children — remains unchanged. Gavin refuses to offer simple comfort, instead leaving the reader to reflect on what real justice would look like in a society built on inequality.

Understanding how Part 3 resolves the novel’s conflicts is essential for the exam. Questions about character, theme or structure will all require you to discuss how the ending reflects Gavin’s wider argument about society, justice and human worth.

The resolution also carries structural significance. The dual timeline that has run throughout the novel finally collapses into a single present moment when Aaron’s parentage is revealed. The worlds of privilege and poverty, which Gavin has kept separate for most of the narrative, are forced to confront each other. This structural convergence mirrors Gavin’s thematic argument: the wealthy cannot remain insulated from the suffering their social system creates. The truth will eventually emerge, even if it takes years.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When writing about the novel’s resolution in the exam, avoid simply saying ‘it has a happy ending.’ The ending is deliberately complex. Show the examiner you understand this by discussing what is gained (reunion, justice) and what is lost (Meshak’s life, Aaron’s foundling years, the other buried babies). This kind of balanced, nuanced analysis — acknowledging complexity rather than simplifying — is what earns top AO1 marks. Always connect the ending to Gavin’s broader point about 18th-century society.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The revelation of Aaron’s parentage resolves the dramatic irony that has run through the novel, merging the two timelines and bringing the Ashbrook world into contact with the foundling world.
  • Thomas Ledbury’s death in the rescue is the novel’s act of physical sacrifice; Meshak’s arc ends peacefully in the Epilogue — together they challenge how society measures human worth.
  • The ending offers qualified justice: Aaron is reunited with his parents and Otis's crimes are exposed, but Thomas Ledbury is dead, years are lost, Otis/Gaddarn disappears without definitive punishment, and the system that enabled the crimes remains unchanged.

lessons.title: Character Analysis
lessons.description: In-depth analysis of Meshak, Otis, Alexander, Aaron, Melissa, Thomas Ledbury and Mrs Lynch.
lessons.content_html:
Character Analysis in Coram Boy

For the Edexcel exam, you may be asked to write about how Gavin presents a specific character or how characters are used to explore a theme. In a closed-book exam, you do not need to remember exact quotations word-for-word, but you must be able to refer to specific moments, describe key scenes and explain how characters develop across the novel. This lesson examines the seven most important characters.

Meshak

Meshak is arguably the novel’s most important character. He has a learning disability, is entirely dependent on his father Otis, and is haunted by the babies he has been forced to bury. Despite this, he is the character who shows the greatest moral courage. When he saves Alexander and Melissa’s baby, he defies the only authority he has ever known. His act of protecting baby Aaron — defying his murderous father Otis — demonstrates that goodness is not dependent on intelligence, social status or wealth.

Key Fact

Gavin presents Meshak as a subversive character — the person society would dismiss as least capable is the one who performs the novel’s most heroic acts. This is Gavin’s central argument about human worth.

Otis Gardiner

Otis is the novel’s primary antagonist. He is calculating, ruthless and without remorse. Unlike many literary villains, Otis is not driven by grand ambition or ideology — he simply wants money. His evil is mundane, which makes it more frightening. He treats child trafficking as a business transaction and controls Meshak through fear and violence. Gavin uses Otis to show that the worst evil often hides behind ordinariness.

Alexander is the privileged son of Sir William Ashbrook. His defining characteristic is his passion for music, which puts him in conflict with his father’s expectations. Alexander eventually defies Sir William to study under Handel in London. His relationship with Melissa produces Aaron, though Alexander believes the child died. Alexander represents the theme of duty versus individual desire, and his story shows how even the privileged are constrained by the class system’s rigid expectations.

Aaron (Toby)

Aaron grows up at the Foundling Hospital under the name Toby, unaware of his true parentage. His extraordinary singing voice — inherited from Alexander — is what eventually draws attention to him and leads to the revelation of his identity. Aaron represents the novel’s exploration of identity: he is defined by others throughout the story (as a foundling, as a singer, as Alexander’s son) and must ultimately reconcile these identities. His character asks the question: who are we if we do not know where we come from?

Melissa is the daughter of a local family who falls in love with Alexander. When she becomes pregnant, the shame falls entirely on her — in 18th-century England, an unmarried mother faced social ruin. The baby is taken from her and given to Otis. Melissa bears the emotional cost of the class system’s double standards: Alexander’s reputation survives, while she carries the grief in silence. Gavin uses Melissa to expose the sexual double standard of Georgian society, where the consequences of an illegitimate child fell almost exclusively on the mother.

Thomas Ledbury

Thomas is Alexander’s childhood friend and a key figure in connecting the Ashbrook world to the wider narrative. He represents loyalty and decency — values that contrast with Otis’s treachery. Thomas is shot and killed by Gaddarn (Otis) during the rescue of Aaron; his death is one of the novel's most shocking moments and’s storylines together. While not as dramatically complex as Meshak or Otis, Thomas functions as a plot connector whose reliability throws the dysfunction of other characters into sharp relief.

Key Fact

Mrs Lynch is complicit in Otis’s crimes. She helps collect babies and maintain the pretence that they are being taken to the Foundling Hospital. Gavin uses Mrs Lynch to show that evil requires accomplices — Otis could not have operated alone. Her character demonstrates that turning a blind eye to injustice is itself a form of moral failure.

Sir William is not a villain, but he represents the rigid values of the Georgian upper class. He expects Alexander to follow a respectable career and dismisses his son’s musical ambitions. His insistence on duty and respectability reflects a class system where individual desires are subordinated to family reputation. Gavin uses Sir William to show that even well-meaning parents can damage their children by imposing the values of their social class.

Character as Theme

Each character in Coram Boy functions as part of Gavin’s wider argument about class, morality and human worth. When writing about characters in the exam, always connect your analysis to these broader themes. The strongest exam responses do not just describe what a character does — they explain what the character represents and why Gavin chose to present them in that way.

Notice how Gavin pairs and contrasts characters to develop her argument. Meshak and Otis are father and son, yet they represent opposite moral poles. Alexander and Aaron are father and son separated by class, yet united by music. Melissa and Mrs Lynch are both women caught in systems that exploit them, yet one is a victim and the other a willing accomplice. These pairings are deliberate — they allow Gavin to test her themes from multiple angles and create a morally complex world.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In a closed-book exam, you cannot look up quotations. Instead, refer to specific moments: ‘When Meshak sees the baby and describes it as an angel…’ or ‘At the point where Otis orders Meshak to bury the child…’ This shows the examiner you know the text well without needing exact wording. Always analyse what the character reveals about Gavin’s themes, not just what they do. For example: ‘Gavin uses Meshak to argue that moral worth is independent of social status, challenging the 18th-century class hierarchy.’
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Meshak is the novel’s moral centre — the character society dismisses as worthless performs the most courageous acts, challenging assumptions about human value.
  • Otis represents the banality of evil — his villainy is mundane and profit-driven, made possible by a society that turns a blind eye to the exploitation of children.
  • Each character embodies a facet of Gavin’s argument about class and morality: Alexander (duty vs. passion), Melissa (the sexual double standard), Aaron (identity without origins), Mrs Lynch (complicity in evil).

lessons.title: Structure, Setting & Narrative Technique
lessons.description: Dual timeline, multiple perspectives, Gothic elements and music as structural motif.
lessons.content_html:
Structure and Narrative Technique

For the Edexcel exam, understanding how Gavin tells the story is just as important as understanding what happens. Questions may ask you to explore how Gavin uses structure, setting or narrative techniques to present ideas. This lesson equips you with the analytical vocabulary and structural awareness to write confidently about form and craft.

The Dual Timeline

Coram Boy is structured around a dual timeline. Part 1 is set in 1741 and follows Meshak and Otis alongside the Ashbrook family. Part 2 jumps forward to 1750 — a nine-year gap and follows Aaron at the Foundling Hospital. Part 3 brings these timelines together when Aaron’s true identity is revealed. This structure creates sustained dramatic irony — the reader knows the connection between the two timelines long before the characters do.

Key Fact

The dual timeline is not just a way of organising events — it is a structural argument. By separating the privileged Ashbrook world from the foundling world, Gavin forces the reader to see how class divides keep people apart even when they are intimately connected.

Multiple Perspectives

Gavin uses a third-person omniscient narrator who moves between different characters’ perspectives. We see events through Meshak’s bewildered, emotional viewpoint; through Otis’s cold, calculating mind; through Alexander’s conflicted ambition; and through Aaron’s search for identity. This shifting perspective allows Gavin to build empathy for multiple characters simultaneously and to create tension by revealing information to the reader that individual characters do not have.

The most powerful use of perspective is through Meshak. When we see the buried babies through his eyes, the horror is intensified because Meshak does not intellectualise or rationalise what he sees — he simply feels it. His emotional directness cuts through any distance the reader might otherwise maintain.

Gavin draws on the Gothic tradition throughout Coram Boy. The landscapes Meshak and Otis travel through are dark, isolated and threatening. The buried babies create an atmosphere of horror that borders on the supernatural — Meshak hears them crying, and the reader is never entirely sure whether this is psychological trauma or something more. The Gothic elements serve a thematic purpose: they prevent the reader from distancing themselves from the cruelty. Gavin uses Gothic imagery to insist that the reader feels the horror of child trafficking rather than merely understanding it intellectually.

Setting as Theme

Every major setting in the novel carries thematic significance. Ashbrook House represents privilege, tradition and the constraints of class. The open roads where Otis and Meshak travel represent lawlessness, danger and the margins of society. The Foundling Hospital represents institutional care — safety without love, rescue without identity. London represents opportunity and culture (through Handel and music) but also the anonymous cruelty of a large city where children can disappear.

Key Fact

Gavin uses settings symbolically: each location represents a different relationship between society and children. Ashbrook House protects its own children through privilege; the Foundling Hospital protects abandoned children through charity; the open road offers no protection at all. The novel asks which model of care is adequate — and the answer is none of them.

Music as Structural Motif

Music is not just a theme in Coram Boy — it functions as a structural motif that binds the novel together. Alexander’s passion for music in Part 1 connects to Aaron’s singing voice in Part 2, with Handel as the bridging figure. Gavin uses the Messiah performances at the Foundling Hospital to bring characters physically together. Music also provides the novel’s emotional register — moments of beauty and transcendence that contrast with the darkness of the child-trafficking plot.

Gavin weaves real historical facts into the fiction so seamlessly that the line between history and invention becomes blurred. Thomas Coram, Handel, the Foundling Hospital and the practice of baby farming are all real — Meshak, Otis, Alexander and Aaron are fictional. By grounding her fictional characters in real historical settings and institutions, Gavin gives the novel the weight of historical truth. This technique makes the reader feel that these events could have happened, which intensifies the emotional impact. For AO3, you can discuss how Gavin uses historical research to create verisimilitude — making the fictional world feel authentic.

Dramatic Irony as a Structural Tool

The most sustained structural technique in Coram Boy is dramatic irony. From Part 1, the reader knows that Meshak saved Alexander and Melissa’s baby. Throughout Part 2, the reader watches Aaron grow up at the Foundling Hospital, knowing his true parentage while he does not. This creates a constant undercurrent of tension: the reader is waiting for the characters to discover what we already know. Gavin sustains this irony across hundreds of pages, which is a remarkable structural achievement — the resolution in Part 3, when the truth finally emerges, is powerful precisely because the reader has been anticipating it for so long.

Being able to discuss structure, setting and narrative technique gives your essay analytical depth. Examiners reward students who can explain how Gavin achieves her effects, not just describe what happens in the story.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When writing about structure or technique, use phrases like: ‘Gavin structures the novel as a dual timeline to create sustained dramatic irony’ or ‘The shift in perspective to Meshak forces the reader to confront the horror emotionally rather than intellectually.’ These phrases demonstrate that you understand how the writer achieves effects (a key requirement for AO1). Always link technique to meaning — explaining why Gavin makes a particular structural choice earns higher marks than simply identifying the technique.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The dual timeline creates dramatic irony and structurally mirrors the class divide, keeping the privileged and marginalised worlds separate until Part 3.
  • Gothic elements, multiple perspectives and symbolic settings all serve Gavin’s thematic purpose — preventing the reader from distancing themselves from the horror of child exploitation.
  • Music functions as a structural motif that connects the novel’s two parts, two generations and two social worlds, arguing that talent and beauty transcend class.

lessons.title: Key Themes & Exam Technique
lessons.description: Childhood, class, good versus evil, music, parentage and identity — plus Edexcel exam technique.
lessons.content_html:
Key Themes in Coram Boy

This lesson draws together the novel’s key themes and shows you how to write about them effectively in your English Literature exam. For a modern-text essay, you will typically be asked to write one extended response in which you explore a theme, character, relationship or event. Your response needs to demonstrate a critical personal response with textual evidence, understanding of context, and accurate writing. Check your exam board’s specimen paper for the exact format and mark allocation.

Childhood and Innocence

Coram Boy is fundamentally a novel about what society owes its children. Gavin presents childhood as a state of innocence that is systematically destroyed by the adult world. The buried babies are the most extreme symbol of this, but the theme extends further: Aaron grows up without knowing his parents; the foundling children are institutionalised and given new identities; even Alexander, who is privileged, has his childhood passion for music crushed by his father’s expectations. Gavin uses childhood as the lens through which every other theme is examined.

Key Fact

The theme of childhood is not just about children — it tests every adult character’s morality. Otis destroys children for profit; Meshak sacrifices himself for a child; the Foundling Hospital saves children but strips their identity. How each character treats children reveals their moral character.

Class and Poverty

The rigid class hierarchy of 18th-century England shapes every character’s life. Alexander’s wealth gives him choices (even if his father constrains them); Aaron’s foundling status means he has no family name, no inheritance and limited prospects; Meshak exists at the very bottom of society, with a disability that makes him even more vulnerable. Gavin uses the class system to show how a person’s birth determines their life chances — and then challenges this by showing that moral worth has nothing to do with social position.

The conflict between good and evil in Coram Boy is not a simple battle between heroes and villains. Otis is clearly evil, but his evil is enabled by a society that turns a blind eye. Meshak is clearly good, but his goodness is trapped within a system of exploitation. The novel suggests that evil is not just the actions of individuals like Otis — it is the complicity of a society that allows vulnerable people to be exploited. Good exists in the novel, but it always comes at a cost: Meshak’s sacrifice, Handel’s charity, Thomas Coram’s decades of campaigning.

Music and Art

Music represents everything that transcends the material world: beauty, talent, emotional truth and the possibility of redemption. Alexander defies his class to pursue music; Aaron’s voice proves his worth beyond his foundling status; Handel’s Messiah literally brings people together at the Foundling Hospital. Gavin uses music to argue that art has the power to cut across class, connect generations and reveal the inner worth of individuals that society would otherwise overlook.

Key Fact

Music connects to every major theme in the novel. It is a class leveller (Aaron’s talent transcends his foundling status), an identity marker (connecting father and son), and a symbol of redemption (beauty surviving amid exploitation). In the exam, the motif of music is one of the most versatile analytical tools you have.

Parentage and Identity

The question of parentage drives the entire plot. Aaron does not know who he is; Alexander does not know his son is alive; Melissa grieves for a child she believes is dead. The Foundling Hospital strips children of their birth names, creating a system where identity is institutional rather than familial. Gavin asks whether identity is determined by birth, by upbringing, or by individual character — and through Aaron and Meshak, she suggests it is the latter.

A modern-text essay question will typically give you a short prompt or quotation and ask you to write an essay exploring a character, theme or aspect of the novel. Here is a proven structure:

Introduction (2–3 sentences): Define the theme or character focus. State your argument clearly. Reference any quotation provided.

Main paragraphs (3–4): Each paragraph should make one analytical point. Use the PEEL structure: Point → Evidence → Explanation → Link. Evidence means referring to specific moments (if the exam is closed-book, describe the scene rather than quoting exactly). Explanation must include both close analysis and connection to context.

Conclusion (2–3 sentences): Summarise your argument. Offer a final evaluative statement — how far do you agree with the prompt? What is Gavin’s overall message?

Mistake 1: Narrative retelling. Do not retell the story. The examiner knows the plot. Focus on how and why Gavin presents events, not just what happens.

Mistake 2: Bolted-on context. Do not write a separate ‘context paragraph’. Embed contextual knowledge within your analysis: ‘Gavin draws on the historical reality of baby farming to present Otis as a product of a society that commodified children.’

Mistake 3: Ignoring the prompt. If the question gives you a quotation or statement, you must respond to it — agree, disagree or partially agree. Use it as the springboard for your argument.

Mistake 4: Vague analysis. Do not write ‘This shows the reader…’ without specifying what it shows and why it matters. Be precise about Gavin’s purpose.

With a thorough understanding of the novel’s themes, characters, structure and historical context, you are well prepared to tackle any question the examiner sets. Remember: the best essays are the ones that show independent thinking, precise analysis and confident use of contextual knowledge.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Time management is critical in the Edexcel exam. Section B is worth 40 marks, and you should spend approximately 50–55 minutes on it within the 1 hour 45 minute paper (after completing Section A on Shakespeare). Plan for 5 minutes of planning, 40 minutes of writing and 5 minutes of checking your SPaG. Always choose the question where you can make the strongest argument — read both options carefully before deciding. AO4 (SPaG) is worth 8 marks, so accurate spelling, punctuation and use of literary terminology matters.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The novel’s key themes — childhood, class, good versus evil, music and identity — are all interconnected. Music links to class, identity and redemption; childhood tests every adult character’s morality; the class system enables both exploitation and complicity.
  • In the Edexcel exam, always respond to the quotation, embed context within analysis (not as a separate paragraph), and focus on how Gavin presents ideas rather than retelling the story.
  • Use the PEEL structure for each paragraph: Point, Evidence (describe specific moments), Explanation (analyse technique + context), Link to the question. This is the most reliable route to high marks.

glossary_terms.definition: The quality of being free from moral wrong or corruption, associated in the novel with children and with Meshak.
The system of social ranking based on birth, wealth and family name that determined life chances in 18th-century England.
Behaviour that allows harmful practices to continue by failing to challenge or prevent them.
The act of being saved or liberated from suffering, sin or wrongdoing.
A person's origins, including who their parents are and the circumstances of their birth.
